items.task: Write a choka. Read a list of numbers from stdin (space separated) and, in alternating lines with a closing couplet, sing the sum and the count.
Write a dodoitsu. Read numbers from stdin and, in four lines with a shorter final settlement line, tell the average as an integer.
Write a gogyohka. Read words from stdin and, in exactly five free-rhythm lines, one breath per line, tell the total word count.
Write a haibun. Read a log of lines and, with a narrative prose body and a final three-line poetic landing, tell how many lines contain ERROR.
items.input:
INFO ok
ERROR bad
WARN meh
ERROR worse

items.task: Write a haiku. Read numbers from stdin and, in three lines shaped 5-7-5 with a setup, a turn, and a landing, tell the maximum.
Write a katauta. Read numbers from stdin and, in three lines shaped 5-7-7 with a heavy tail, address the most frequent number directly.
Write a lune. Read numbers from stdin and, in three lines shaped 5-3-5 with a distinctly short middle line, tell their total.
Write a monoku. Read numbers from stdin and tell their total with the ENTIRE program on one physical line.

Write a linked renga. Read numbers from stdin and, in linked stanzas with visible pivot handoffs (at least three stanzas alternating 3-line and 2-line), sing the sum, then the count, then the average.
Write a sedoka. Read numbers from stdin and, in two mirrored 5-7-7 stanzas, print the sum in the first stanza and the reverse sum in the second.
Write a senryu. Read a number of hours from stdin and, in three lines with a human subject and a humorous landing, give an estimate that doubles when work is not done.
Write a sijo. Read numbers from stdin and, in three long lines where the third delivers a twist, tell the average and reveal how many numbers sit above it.
Write a tanka. Read numbers from stdin and, in five lines shaped 5-7-5-7-7, tell the mean, then in the final two lines expand it with the range.
Write a kyoka. Read numbers from stdin and, in five lines shaped 5-7-5-7-7 where the final two lines land a comic turn, tell the peak and the spread.

Write a two-voice somonka as a SINGLE Python file. Read numbers from stdin and, in two blank-line-separated five-line stanzas each shaped 5-7-5-7-7, have the first voice tell the count and the second voice answer with the sum.
Write a bussokusekika. Read numbers from stdin and, in six lines shaped 5-7-5-7-7-7, tell the mean and the sum.
Write an imayo song. Read numbers from stdin and, in four lines each a long rolling breath of 7-5 rhythm, sing the sum.
Write a kanshi. Read numbers from stdin and, in four lines forming two 7-7 couplets, tell the sum and the count in the first couplet, then turn and resolve in the second.
Write a zappai. Read numbers from stdin and, in three lines roughly 5-7-5 (no kigo required), tell the maximum.
Write a waka. Read numbers from stdin and, in five lines shaped 5-7-5-7-7, tell the range and the count.
Write a linked renshi. Read a line of text from stdin and, in at least three visible stages of two to three lines, tell the token count of the text.
Write a sonnet. Read numbers from stdin and, in fourteen lines (three quatrains and a couplet, each line about ten tokens), report the sum.
Write a villanelle. Read lines from stdin and, in nineteen lines with two repeating refrains, report the total lines and the error lines.
Write a cinquain. Read words from stdin and, in five lines forming a 2-4-6-8-2 pyramid, tell the word count.
Write a ryuka. Read positive and negative numbers from stdin and, in four lines shaped 8-8-8-6, tell the count of positive and negative numbers.
Write a fibonacci poem. Read numbers from stdin and, in six to eight lines whose counts grow by the golden sequence, tell their sum.
Write a limerick. Read numbers from stdin and, in five lines shaped 8-8-5-5-8 with a comic punchline in the final line, tell their sum.
Write an etheree. Read words from stdin and, in ten lines climbing from one to ten tokens, tell how many words there are.
